title: After Modernism
description: Postwar to present — irony, metafiction, exhaustion

concepts.title: Defining Postmodernism
concepts.contentHtml:
Postmodernism in literature is the loose set of post-1945 (especially post-1960) styles that succeeded modernism. The term is contested and slippery. It covers very different writers and modes.

Common features: irony, metafiction, fragmentation, mixing high and low culture, suspicion of grand narratives, playful relationship to genre, intertextuality.

The label has been more useful for grouping than for defining. Many writers called postmodernist (Pynchon, Barth, Calvino, Borges) reject or modify the label.

concepts.title: After Modernism
concepts.contentHtml:
Modernism (Joyce, Woolf, Eliot, Faulkner) had pushed certain techniques to their limits — stream of consciousness, mythic structure, allusive density, fragmented form.

Postwar writers faced a problem: how to write after these had been done. Several responses.

Some absorbed modernist techniques into more accessible form (Bellow, Updike). Some pushed further into experiment (Beckett's late prose). Some mocked the seriousness (Barth's The Floating Opera). Some turned to popular forms with new self-awareness (Pynchon's pulp gestures).

concepts.title: Lyotard and Grand Narratives
concepts.contentHtml:
The philosophical sense of postmodernism comes largely from Jean-François Lyotard's The Postmodern Condition (1979).

Lyotard's definition: 'incredulity toward metanarratives.' The grand stories modernity told about itself — progress, science, Marxism, Christianity, the Enlightenment — had lost their unquestioned authority. What replaced them was a plurality of smaller narratives, each with limited claims.

Whether postmodernism describes literature, philosophy, architecture, or society as a whole has been debated. The term is broad to the point of vagueness.

concepts.title: Jameson and Cultural Logic
concepts.contentHtml:
Fredric Jameson's Postmodernism, or, the Cultural Logic of Late Capitalism (1991) gave the term its most influential cultural-political analysis.

Jameson argued postmodernism wasn't just a style — it was the cultural logic of late capitalism. Pastiche replacing parody (no stable original to mock). Depthlessness replacing depth. Schizophrenic time replacing linear narrative.

The book became a touchstone. Whether it's persuasive in detail or not, it provided a vocabulary for thinking about post-1960s culture in relation to economic conditions.

concepts.title: Whether Postmodernism Is Over
concepts.contentHtml:
By the 2000s, many critics were arguing postmodernism had ended. David Foster Wallace's 'E Unibus Pluram' (1993) attacked postmodern irony as exhausted and called for new sincerity. The post-2000 'New Sincerity' movement (Wallace, George Saunders, Dave Eggers) tried to write past postmodern detachment.

Other replacements proposed: metamodernism (oscillation between sincerity and irony); post-postmodernism; digimodernism (literature shaped by digital reading).

The honest assessment: postmodernism's specific moment (roughly 1960s-90s) has passed, but its techniques and concerns persist in transformed forms. The label has become historical rather than current.

concepts.title: Borges
concepts.contentHtml:
Jorge Luis Borges (1899-1986), Argentine writer, was the most influential precursor of literary postmodernism. His short fictions of the 1940s — Ficciones (1944), The Aleph (1949) — created the templates much of subsequent experimental fiction would draw on.

Borges wrote almost no novels. His fictions are short — usually 5-15 pages — and densely conceptual. Each typically poses a philosophical or mathematical puzzle in narrative form.

He went blind in middle age. He worked as a librarian, then director of the Argentine National Library. He never won the Nobel — a long-running scandal of the prize.

concepts.title: Major Stories
concepts.contentHtml:
'The Library of Babel': the universe is a library containing every possible book. The implications.

'The Garden of Forking Paths': time as branching alternatives, every choice splitting the universe.

'Pierre Menard, Author of the Quixote': a 20th-century French writer recomposes chapters of Don Quixote word-for-word, and the narrator judges them richer than Cervantes's for having been written in the 20th century.

'Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius': an imagined world's encyclopedia begins to replace the real one.

'The Aleph': a point in space containing all other points.

Each story takes a single conceptual idea and works it out as fiction with extraordinary economy.

concepts.title: What Borges Did
concepts.contentHtml:
Borges introduced moves that became postmodern staples.

Metafiction: stories about texts, libraries, encyclopedias, fictional authors. The story comments on its own fictionality.

Erudition as fiction: invented references, fake citations, footnotes to nonexistent books. The reader can't tell the real from the made-up.

Conceptual compression: an idea that would take a novel for most writers gets eight pages.

Genre dissolution: detective story, fantasy, philosophy, essay all blend together.

Almost every postmodern writer has read Borges. Calvino, Eco, Pynchon, Auster, Bolaño all show his influence directly.

concepts.title: Other Latin American Predecessors
concepts.contentHtml:
Borges was part of a broader Latin American moment.

Adolfo Bioy Casares (Argentine, 1914-1999): Borges's friend and frequent collaborator. The Invention of Morel (1940) anticipated virtual reality and reality TV.

Juan Rulfo (Mexican, 1917-1986): Pedro Páramo (1955), a short novel told through fragmentary voices — including the dead. A foundational text for magical realism.

Alejo Carpentier (Cuban, 1904-1980): coined the term 'lo real maravilloso' for the magical-real of Latin American experience. The Kingdom of This World (1949).

Julio Cortázar (Argentine, 1914-1984): Hopscotch (1963), a novel readers can read in multiple orders.

concepts.title: Why Latin America
concepts.contentHtml:
Why did so much innovative postmodern fiction come from Latin America?

Several theories. The continent's history of colonisation, dictatorship, and migration produced experiences hard to fit into European realism. Writers had access to European modernism (often via Paris) plus indigenous and folk traditions European writers didn't share. The Spanish-language publishing industry was integrated across countries in ways that supported regional literary movements.

The result: Latin American writers anticipated and shaped what would become postmodern technique decades before North American postmodernism named itself. Borges, Cortázar, Rulfo, Bioy were doing it in the 1940s and 50s.

The 'Boom' of the 1960s exported these techniques globally. Subsequent generations have continued the tradition.

title: American Postmodernism
description: Pynchon, DeLillo, Barth — paranoia and play

concepts.title: American Postmodern Fiction
concepts.contentHtml:
The American postmodern novel emerged in the 1960s. Multiple writers, no unified programme. Common features: encyclopedic sweep, paranoid plotting, comic-conspiratorial tone, mixing high theory with pop culture.

Major figures: Thomas Pynchon, Don DeLillo, John Barth, Robert Coover, William Gaddis, Joseph Heller, Kurt Vonnegut, John Hawkes.

Most were men, white, mid-century. The category has been criticised for its narrow demographic. The basic moves — paranoid plotting, metafiction, encyclopedic ambition — also appear in writers from other traditions.

concepts.title: Pynchon
concepts.contentHtml:
Thomas Pynchon (b. 1937) is the most influential American postmodern novelist. His major books: V. (1963), The Crying of Lot 49 (1966), Gravity's Rainbow (1973), Vineland (1990), Mason & Dixon (1997), Against the Day (2006), Inherent Vice (2009), Bleeding Edge (2013).

Gravity's Rainbow is his canonical work. 760 pages, set during and after WWII, organised around the V-2 rocket, with hundreds of characters and constant philosophical-historical-conspiratorial digression.

Pynchon has been famously reclusive. No public interviews; few photographs. His writing — comic, paranoid, dense, allusive, deeply musical — sits at the centre of what 'postmodern fiction' came to mean.

concepts.title: Barth and Metafiction
concepts.contentHtml:
John Barth (1930-2024) was the theorist of American metafiction. His 1967 essay 'The Literature of Exhaustion' argued the realist novel had used up its possibilities; new fiction would have to operate self-consciously about its own conditions.

His novels practised what the essay preached. The Sot-Weed Factor (1960), Giles Goat-Boy (1966), Lost in the Funhouse (1968) — all explicitly metafictional, often parodying earlier literary forms.

Robert Coover's The Universal Baseball Association (1968) and The Public Burning (1977); William Gass's formal experiments — these belong to the same metafictional moment.

concepts.title: DeLillo
concepts.contentHtml:
Don DeLillo (b. 1936) developed a different mode — sentence-by-sentence philosophical observation rather than encyclopedic plotting.

White Noise (1985): a college professor's family in a small town, increasingly disoriented by media saturation and an 'airborne toxic event.' Crystallised the postmodern sense of dread-and-detachment.

Libra (1988): a novelistic reconstruction of Lee Harvey Oswald.

Underworld (1997): an 800-page sweep through American Cold War decades. Many critics' pick for the great late-20th-century American novel.

DeLillo's sentences are individually quotable in ways Pynchon's aren't. Less manic, more meditative, equally postmodern.

concepts.title: After the Big Postmoderns
concepts.contentHtml:
By the 1990s a generation came of age in dialogue with Pynchon, DeLillo, and Barth.

David Foster Wallace (1962-2008): Infinite Jest (1996). Pynchonian length and ambition with explicit New Sincerity ambitions against postmodern irony.

Jonathan Franzen (b. 1959): the social novel's return after Wallace's wake.

Jennifer Egan, Colson Whitehead, George Saunders: continued postmodern moves in transformed form.

The big-American-postmodern novel as a recognisable type has faded. Its techniques (metafiction, paranoia, genre play) survive in many contemporary writers, just no longer as a programmatic movement.

title: The Latin American Boom
description: García Márquez, Cortázar, Vargas Llosa — magic realism

concepts.title: What the Boom Was
concepts.contentHtml:
The Latin American Boom was the international success of a generation of Spanish-language novelists in the 1960s and 1970s. Their work, reaching world readership through translation, became one of the major literary phenomena of the 20th century.

Major figures: Gabriel García Márquez (Colombian), Julio Cortázar (Argentine), Mario Vargas Llosa (Peruvian), Carlos Fuentes (Mexican).

Plus older writers (Borges, Rulfo) read alongside them, and slightly younger ones (Manuel Puig, Cabrera Infante, José Donoso) sometimes included.

concepts.title: García Márquez
concepts.contentHtml:
Gabriel García Márquez (1927-2014, Nobel 1982) wrote the central Boom novel. One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967) traces the Buendía family across a century in the fictional town of Macondo.

The book combines realist family-saga structure with elements of myth, magic, and folk legend. Children born with pig tails; rain that lasts years; characters ascending bodily into heaven; ghosts who continue family arguments.

The opening line — 'Many years later, as he faced the firing squad, Colonel Aureliano Buendía was to remember that distant afternoon when his father took him to discover ice' — has become one of the most quoted in Latin American literature.

The novel sold tens of millions worldwide. It defined what international readers expected of Latin American fiction for the next thirty years.

concepts.title: Magical Realism
concepts.contentHtml:
Magical realism — the literary mode in which the magical is treated as ordinary, the ordinary as wondrous — has roots in Carpentier and Rulfo but reached its widest audience through García Márquez.

The technique: events that violate physical or causal laws are narrated in matter-of-fact prose, with no special framing. Characters react to them as they would to any event. The reader is invited to accept what realism would refuse.

The mode was not invented in Latin America (precursors: Kafka, Bulgakov), but became identified with it. Subsequent magical-realist writers in many countries — Rushdie, Toni Morrison, Allende, Murakami in some moods — work in the lineage García Márquez popularised.

concepts.title: Other Boom Writers
concepts.contentHtml:
Julio Cortázar: Hopscotch (1963), a 'novel that can be read at least two ways' — chapters can be followed in numerical order or in a sequence the author provides. Plus the masterly short stories of Bestiary, End of the Game, Blow-Up.

Mario Vargas Llosa (Nobel 2010): The Time of the Hero (1963), Conversation in the Cathedral (1969), The War of the End of the World (1981). Tighter, more political, more realist than García Márquez.

Carlos Fuentes: The Death of Artemio Cruz (1962), Terra Nostra (1975).

Each had a distinctive style. The grouping was partly publishing convenience — they were translated and marketed together.

concepts.title: After the Boom
concepts.contentHtml:
Latin American fiction continued after the Boom but shifted modes.

Roberto Bolaño (Chilean, 1953-2003): The Savage Detectives (1998), 2666 (2004 posthumous). Bolaño wrote against the Boom — against magical realism, against its commercial template. His mode: long, dark, formally restless.

Clarice Lispector (Brazilian, 1920-1977): from before the Boom but rediscovered after. The most distinctive philosophical-mystical writer in Portuguese.

César Aira, Mariana Enriquez, Samanta Schweblin, Yuri Herrera: contemporary Spanish-language writers operating in modes the Boom didn't anticipate.

Latin American literature is no longer reducible to the Boom. The continent continues to produce major writing in many idioms.

title: Contemporary Voices
description: Sebald, Knausgaard, Ferrante, Adichie — the global novel today

concepts.title: Where Fiction Is Now
concepts.contentHtml:
The 21st-century literary novel has no single dominant mode. Multiple traditions coexist: realism, autofiction, speculative, hybrid, translated work from many languages.

What's clear: literary fiction is more global than ever. Major writers come from everywhere. Translation has expanded as a cultural enterprise. Prize culture (Booker International, Neustadt, the Nobel, the National Book Award translated category) directs attention beyond the major-language markets.

concepts.title: W.G. Sebald
concepts.contentHtml:
W.G. Sebald (1944-2001), German-born, lived and taught in England, wrote in German. Major books: The Emigrants (1992), The Rings of Saturn (1995), Austerlitz (2001).

Sebald's mode is unique. Long sentences. Unbroken paragraphs. Black-and-white photographs scattered through the text. Genre-blurring — part novel, part essay, part travelogue, part memoir. Continual displacement of the narrator across European landscapes.

His subject is largely the Holocaust and what survived of European Jewish life — handled obliquely, through traces rather than direct narration. He died in a car accident at 57. His brief output has had outsized influence on subsequent literary fiction.

concepts.title: Knausgaard and Autofiction
concepts.contentHtml:
Karl Ove Knausgaard (Norwegian, b. 1968) wrote My Struggle (six volumes, 3,500 pages, 2009-11), one of the major autofictional projects in literary history.

The mode: extreme, sometimes tedious detail of his actual life — childhood, his alcoholic father, marriage, fatherhood, friendships, struggles with writing. Fictional shaping is minimal; the project's bet is that sustained attention to ordinary life produces meaning.

Annie Ernaux (French, b. 1940, Nobel 2022): a parallel autofictional project across decades. The Years (2008), her masterpiece, traces French collective experience from 1941 to 2006 through a personal-impersonal voice.

Other major autofiction: Rachel Cusk, Sheila Heti, Ben Lerner, Maggie Nelson, Jenny Offill.

concepts.title: Ferrante
concepts.contentHtml:
Elena Ferrante (Italian, pseudonymous) wrote the four Neapolitan Novels (2011-2014, English 2012-2015). My Brilliant Friend, The Story of a New Name, Those Who Leave and Those Who Stay, The Story of the Lost Child.

The novels follow two friends, Lila and Elena, from childhood in 1950s Naples through old age. Class, gender, education, the city's poverty and violence are continuous presences.

The books became a global phenomenon — over 16 million copies sold, an HBO adaptation, what's been called 'Ferrante fever.' The author has remained pseudonymous despite intense journalistic investigation.

The novels demonstrate that traditional realist long-form fiction, done with sustained intelligence about gender and class, can still command global readership.

concepts.title: The Global Now
concepts.contentHtml:
Other contemporary writers shaping the moment:

Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, Olga Tokarczuk (Polish, Nobel 2018), Han Kang (Korean, Nobel 2024), Mohsin Hamid, Yoko Tawada (Japanese-German), Mariana Enriquez, Mieko Kawakami, Ocean Vuong, Tommy Orange, Natasha Brown, Brandon Taylor.

The list could be much longer. The point: contemporary fiction is more diverse, more international, and more formally varied than at any prior moment.

Whether the contemporary moment will retrospectively look like a coherent period — like 'modernism' or 'the Boom' — or like fragmentation without single direction is unanswerable from inside it. The 21st century is being written.
